anti_patterns: Treating sequencer soft-confirmations as final: triggering irreversible L1 or off-chain actions on unchallenged L2 output instead of waiting out the fraud-proof window or buying finality
Running with no independent verifier: nobody re-executes posted batches, voiding the 1-of-N-honest assumption that secures optimistic stacks
Skipping the forced-inclusion path: leaving users dependent on the hosted sequencer mempool so a halted or censoring sequencer freezes accounts with no L1 deposit escape hatch
Choosing committee-based data availability silently: deploying on AnyTrust/DAC or external DA for cost reasons without disclosing the added trust assumption to users and liquidity providers
Single-provider lock-in with no exit plan: handing chain ownership keys, bridge admin rights, or upgrade authority to the operator instead of retaining them and keeping config portable
Launching a dedicated chain when a shared L2 suffices: paying sequencer, DA-posting, and bridging overhead for an app with no throughput, customization, or gas-token need
avoid_when: Application fits comfortably on a shared public L2 with no custom fee or throughput requirements
Sub-second hard-finality settlement is required (optimistic challenge windows still impose ~7-day withdrawals)
Strict data-residency or sovereignty rules forbid dependence on an external sequencer operator
Team cannot tolerate any additional trusted party beyond the L1 validator set
Transaction volume is too low to justify dedicated sequencer, DA-posting, and monitoring costs
Single-organization internal system with no multi-party or user-facing bridging needs
benefits: Dedicated blockspace: predictable fees and latency isolated from neighboring apps competing on a shared L2
Launch speed: production-grade chain in days via deployment UI instead of months of sequencer, prover, and bridge engineering
Full chain customization: own chain ID, block time, gas limit, custom ERC-20 gas token, permissioning, and precompiles
Inherited parent security: execution scales off-chain while settlement and data availability anchor to Ethereum or an L2 parent
Operated critical path: hosted sequencer, batcher, prover, RPC, explorer, bridge UI, and 24/7 monitoring under an uptime SLA
Coordinated upgrades: provider tests and rolls out upstream OP Stack, Orbit, CDK, or ZK Stack releases instead of the app team tracking them
Ecosystem alignment on demand: opt into Superchain shared bridging, Orbit settlement, AggLayer unified liquidity, or Elastic Chain interop
best_practices: Retain chain ownership: sequencer keys, bridge admin contracts, and upgrade authority stay with the team under an operable-by-provider contract
Validate on testnet first: exercise deposits, withdrawals (including the full challenge window), upgrades, and failover before mainnet
Choose the data-availability layer explicitly: model L1 calldata vs EIP-4844 blobs vs Celestia/EigenDA/Avail/AnyTrust cost against the trust assumption, and disclose it
Run an independent verifier or watcher: re-execute batches and monitor state roots even when the provider operates the sequencer
Keep the forced-inclusion and escape-hatch path tested: users must be able to deposit and exit via the parent chain without sequencer cooperation
Track L1 submission costs per transaction: blob/calliata fees dominate rollup economics; alert and retune batching before margins invert
Negotiate upgrade windows and SLA remedies: test upstream hard forks on testnet, schedule mainnet cutover at low traffic, define credits for missed uptime
Plan the decentralization path: document how the chain moves from a single hosted sequencer to shared or permissionless sequencing
component_types: Sequencer/Batcher: orders L2 transactions, produces blocks, posts compressed batches to the data-availability layer
Prover (ZK stacks): generates validity proofs for state transitions; fraud-proof dispute contracts on optimistic stacks
Data-Availability Writer: routes batch data to L1 calldata, EIP-4844 blobs, or modular DA (Celestia, EigenDA, Avail, AnyTrust)
Settlement/Bridge Contracts: rollup manager, inbox, and L1-L2 message bridge deployed on the parent chain
Full Nodes and RPC Fleet: autoscaling read replicas serving wallets, indexers, and dapps with usage metering
Block Explorer and Indexer: searchable chain state, bridge activity, and developer APIs bundled with the deployment
Telemetry and Alerting: sequencer latency, block production, L1 submission cost, and bridge dashboards with on-call response
Upgrade Coordinator: staged rollout of upstream framework releases from testnet to mainnet
context: A product team needs its own application-specific chain with custom fees, throughput, and governance, but building rollup infrastructure from scratch demands deep Ethereum client engineering: sequencer design, fraud- or validity-proof systems, data-availability integration, and bridge security. Since the OP Stack (late 2022) and Arbitrum Orbit (2023) open-sourced modular rollup codebases, the hard part shifted from writing rollup code to operating it reliably at scale. Rollup-as-a-Service applies when a team wants a dedicated L2 (settling to Ethereum) or L3 (settling to an L2 parent) without running the sequencer, prover, bridge, and monitoring stack itself: the team picks a framework, settlement layer, data-availability layer, and chain parameters, and a managed platform (Caldera, Conduit, AltLayer, Alchemy Rollups, Zeeve) provisions and operates the chain while the team keeps chain ownership and governance.
design_principles: Modular stack selection: execution, settlement, data availability, proving, and sequencing are independent choices matched to cost and security goals
Security inheritance by construction: the rollup is only as safe as its parent settlement plus its data-availability guarantees; every cost optimization must name its trust delta
Team-owned chain, provider-operated infrastructure: ownership keys and governance never transfer to the operator
Escape hatches before convenience: forced inclusion and parent-chain exits must work even if the hosted sequencer halts
Upgrade transparency: upstream framework changes are staged on testnet and cut over on a coordinated schedule, never silently

tradeoffs: Centralized sequencer bottleneck: a single hosted sequencer is a liveness and censorship risk until decentralized sequencing matures
Data-availability trust ladder: AnyTrust committees and external DA layers cut posting costs dramatically but add availability assumptions weaker than Ethereum L1
Optimistic finality latency: fraud-proof challenge windows (~7 days) fix withdrawal times regardless of how fast the managed sequencer confirms
Provider dependence: operational reliance on one vendor's tooling, upgrade cadence, and pricing creates migration friction even when keys are team-owned
Recurring cost floor: platform fees plus L1 blob/calldata posting must stay below the saved DevOps cost, and L1 fee spikes pass through
Fragmented liquidity and onboarding: users must bridge assets to a new network instead of composing with established L2 liquidity
Ecosystem coupling: Superchain, Orbit, AggLayer, or Elastic interop benefits tie the chain's roadmap to that framework's governance
use_cases: Gaming chain needing dedicated blockspace and custom gas token (e.g. Xai Games-style app-chain)
DeFi protocol isolating MEV and fee policy from shared-L2 congestion
Consumer app requiring predictable sub-cent fees via alt-DA while settling to Ethereum
Enterprise settlement layer with permissioned access on a dedicated rollup
L3 settling to Arbitrum One or Base for ecosystem-aligned liquidity and tooling
Multi-chain product family spawning per-segment rollups from one deployment template
